probableCause: Hypothesis: the test is time-dependent. Promotion.isActive() most likely compares the promotion's end date (2026-10-31) with the current system date, for example via LocalDate.now(). The test passes a hard-coded date in the year 2026 and expects isActive() to be true. If the CI run happened after 2026-10-31, the promotion has expired and the assertion fails with no code change. The Promotion class source is not in the evidence, so this cannot be confirmed. A defect in Promotion.isActive() itself is an alternative explanation.
evidence: Failing test: com.acme.export.promotion.PromotionTest#autumnPromotionIsStillActive, with AssertionFailedError: expected: <true> but was: <false>.

PromotionTest.java line 21 builds new Promotion("AUTUMN-26", LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 31)), a fixed calendar date, and line 23 asserts promotion.isActive() is true. The assertion on line 23 is the one that fails.

The sibling test promotionFromThePastIsNotActive (lines 13-16) uses LocalDate.of(2020, 12, 31) and asserts isActive() is false. This suggests isActive() compares the date argument with some notion of 'today', but the evidence does not show how.
The test name 'autumnPromotionIsStillActive' and the hard-coded 2026 date imply the test only holds while the current date is on or before the end date. No clock is injected or fixed in the test.
The stack trace has no frame inside Promotion, so the failure is a plain assertion failure and not an exception thrown by production code.

possibleSolutions.solution: Investigative step: check the date of the failing CI run and the implementation of Promotion.isActive() (whether it uses LocalDate.now(), and whether the comparison is inclusive or exclusive) to confirm or rule out the time-dependence hypothesis.
tradeoffs: Cheap and non-invasive, and it removes the uncertainty before any change is made.
Requires access to the Promotion source and the CI run metadata, which are not in the provided evidence.

possibleSolutions.solution: Make the time source injectable, for example by giving Promotion or isActive() a java.time.Clock or a reference-date parameter, and have the test use a fixed clock.
tradeoffs: Makes the test deterministic and independent of when it runs.
Changes the production API or constructor, so all call sites must be updated and reviewed.

possibleSolutions.solution: Build the test data relative to the current date, for example LocalDate.now().plusDays(30), so the promotion is always in the future.
tradeoffs: Very small change that only touches the test.
The test still depends on the real clock, so it is less deterministic, and it could be flaky around midnight or time-zone boundaries.

possibleSolutions.solution: If the promotion has genuinely expired and the test only documents a past campaign, update or remove the test to match the intended business behaviour.
tradeoffs: Removes a stale test that can only fail with time.
Loses coverage of the 'active promotion' case unless a replacement test is added.

confidenceReason: The test source clearly shows a hard-coded date in 2026 and an assertion that it is active, which is a well-known pattern for tests that fail once a date passes. However, the Promotion implementation, the CI run date and any logs are missing, so the date-expiry explanation remains an inference and a logic bug in isActive() cannot be excluded.
limitations: The source of com.acme.export.promotion.Promotion is not provided, so the logic of isActive() is unknown.
The date and time zone of the CI run are not given, so it cannot be verified whether the run was after 2026-10-31.
No execution log output was available for this test.
No spec or ADR is mapped to PromotionTest or to the classes in the stack trace, so the intended business rules for promotion validity are unknown.
The stack trace shows unusual JUnit frames (Assertions.notEqual called from assertTrue), which may be a rendering artifact; this was not used as evidence for the cause.
